newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - May 20 Fed hike still seen most likely.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - May 20 Fed hike still seen most likely.

text.p: Most economists expect the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates again on May 20, and many said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's speech on Thursday did not change their outlook, a Reuters poll showed.
Nineteen of 26 experts in the United States and Canada forecast a 25-basis-point hike in the federal funds rate when the central bank's policymaking arm convenes later this month.
Seven others said the Fed will hold the key short rate at its current 5.50 percent.
By comparison, 22 of 29 economists polled earlier this week projected a higher funds rate after the May 20 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.

In a speech in New York, Greenspan said the central bank would need to act if economic growth does not show signs of slowing. But he added that economic conditions now were very different from those in 1994 that forced the Fed "to tighten monetary conditions very substantially."
While some analysts read the comments as signaling less chance of a May 20 rate shift, most economists in the survey said it did not impact their interest rate forecasts.
"There's nothing in that speech that would dissuade me from staying with the paradigm I follow when I view Fed activity," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Capacity constraints and labor market tightness remain troubling, making further credit tightening likely, Liro said.
Most survey respondents said their projections for the May meeting were a close call.
John Ryding, managing director and senior economist at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc, said Greenspan intended to provide little insight into the outcome of the next FOMC gathering.
"This time around, I think (Greenspan) has left his options open," he said.

"If Alan Greenspan can go away from giving a speech within two weeks of a crucial FOMC meeting and have the Wall Street Journal and Washington Post write diametrically opposed headlines, he is happy with the job he did," Ryding added.
A few economists focused on the Fed chief's comments that 1997 is not 1994, which they interpreted to mean the Fed has hopes for slower growth and benign inflation.

"You read his speech and he says we're more balanced than we were in 1994," said Larry Dyer, governments strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "Currently, (central bankers) probably feel they need a little more insurance, but I don't think they feel they have to rush with it."

Further out, 22 of 24 experts called for at least 25 basis points of tightening in either May or July. The economists were split over where fed funds would be at yearend, with the average forecast between 5.75 percent and 6.0 percent.
